passages.t: The river and the tree of life
passages.happening:
“Then the angel showed me a river of the water of life, as clear as crystal, flowing from the throne of God and of the Lamb down the middle of the main street of the city” (verses 1-2).

“On either side of the river stood a tree of life, bearing twelve kinds of fruit and yielding a fresh crop for each month. And the leaves of the tree are for the healing of the nations” (verse 2).

“No longer will there be any curse. The throne of God and of the Lamb will be within the city, and His servants will worship Him. They will see His face, and His name will be on their foreheads” (verses 3-4).

“There will be no more night in the city, and they will have no need for the light of a lamp or of the sun. For the Lord God will shine on them, and they will reign forever and ever” (verse 5).
passages.hearers:
This is the last page of the Bible, and it deliberately returns to the first. In Genesis 2 there was a garden, a river flowing out of Eden, and the tree of life. In Genesis 3 came the curse, and humanity was driven out, with cherubim set to guard ‘the way to the tree of life’. Between those pages and this one lie the whole history of Israel, the coming of Jesus, his death and resurrection, and the mission of the church. Here the curse is gone, the tree stands open, and the river flows from God's own throne. The garden has become a garden inside a city.

The river is ‘the water of life’. The Greek word for life here, zōē, means not bare existence but the life that belongs to God and that he shares, the life humanity lost access to in Genesis 3 and receives again here. In the dry lands of the Bible, water was life itself.

The river flows ‘from the throne of God and of the Lamb’. One throne, shared by God and the Lamb.

The tree of life bears fruit every month, and its leaves are ‘for the healing of the nations’. Not Israel only. The nations. The nations that Babylon made drunk, that the beast deceived, that gathered against God, are pictured here being healed. The Greek word for tree, xulon, means wood or tree, and elsewhere in the New Testament it is used for the cross. Many readers have seen a link, though Revelation itself does not draw it.

‘No longer will there be any curse.’ The sentence on the ground in Genesis 3, and the whole history of death and frustration that followed it, is reversed.

‘They will see His face.’ This was the deepest longing of Israel's worship, and also something no one could do and live. God told Moses that no one could see his face and survive. The promise means that the barrier between a holy God and his people is gone. His name on their foreheads means they belong to him, the seal of chapter 7 made complete.

And ‘they will reign forever and ever’. The calling given to humanity in the garden, to rule God's world under him, is restored.
passages.ot:
The garden and the river are Genesis: “And in the middle of the garden were the tree of life and the tree of the knowledge of good and evil” (Genesis 2:9), and “a river flowed out of Eden to water the garden” (Genesis 2:10). Then the way was shut: God “stationed cherubim on the east side of the Garden of Eden, along with a whirling sword of flame to guard the way to the tree of life” (Genesis 3:24).

The river from the temple is Ezekiel's vision: “Each month they will bear fruit, because the water from the sanctuary flows to them. Their fruit will be used for food and their leaves for healing” (Ezekiel 47:12). Zechariah saw “living water will flow out from Jerusalem” (Zechariah 14:8), and the psalm sings, “There is a river whose streams delight the city of God” (Psalm 46:4).

And the face no one could see is God's word to Moses: “You cannot see My face, for no one can see Me and live” (Exodus 33:20).
passages.asks: Ask what it means to you that the Bible ends with healing, and not simply with escape. Ask which nations or peoples you find it hardest to picture being healed by the leaves of that tree. And ask what it would mean for you to long to see God's face more than anything else.

passages.happening:
“Then the angel said to me, ‘These words are faithful and true. The Lord, the God of the spirits of the prophets, has sent His angel to show His servants what must soon take place’” (verse 6).

Then Jesus speaks: “Behold, I am coming soon.” And he speaks of “the one who keeps the words of prophecy in this book” (verse 7).

“And I am John, who heard and saw these things. And when I had heard and seen them, I fell down to worship at the feet of the angel who had shown me these things” (verse 8). The angel stops him: “Do not do that! I am a fellow servant with you and your brothers the prophets, and with those who keep the words of this book. Worship God!” (verse 9).
passages.hearers:
The vision is over. From here to the end, the book's closing words turn from what John saw to how the churches should live while they wait. Many of its phrases repeat the book's opening in chapter 1: ‘what must soon take place’ (1:1), the angel sent to show God's servants, and soon ‘the time is near’ (1:3). The book ends where it began.

The epilogue is a gathering of voices: the angel, Jesus, John, the Spirit and the bride, and the one who hears. Sometimes it is not clear who is speaking. The effect is of a whole church speaking at once.

Three times in this chapter Jesus says he is coming soon (verses 7, 12 and 20). Here the word is joined to a promise for ‘the one who keeps the words of prophecy in this book’. The book was meant to be kept, lived by, not only decoded. The book has seven sayings of blessing in all, and two of them are in this chapter.

John signs his name: ‘I am John, who heard and saw these things’. And then he does again what he did in 19:10. He falls at the angel's feet, and again the angel stops him: “Worship God!” Even at the end, after all he has seen, the seer can be dazzled by the messenger. The angel is a fellow servant with the prophets and with everyone who keeps the book. Only God is to be worshipped.
passages.ot: Unlike this book, Daniel's was to be sealed: “But you, Daniel, shut up these words and seal the book until the time of the end” (Daniel 12:4). John is told the opposite in the next verse. The book of Daniel was kept for a later day; Revelation is opened now.
passages.asks: Ask what it would mean for you to ‘keep’ this book, not only to study it. Ask which messengers, teachers or gifts you are tempted to treat as more than fellow servants. And ask what it means that the book ends by sending you back to worship God.

passages.happening:
“Then he told me, ‘Do not seal up the words of prophecy in this book, because the time is near. Let the unrighteous continue to be unrighteous, and the vile continue to be vile; let the righteous continue to practice righteousness, and the holy continue to be holy’” (verses 10-11).

“Behold, I am coming soon, and My reward is with Me, to give to each one according to what he has done. I am the Alpha and the Omega, the First and the Last, the Beginning and the End” (verses 12-13).

Then a saying about “those who wash their robes, so that they may have the right to the tree of life and may enter the city by its gates” (verse 14). “But outside are the dogs, the sorcerers, the sexually immoral, the murderers, the idolaters, and everyone who loves and practices falsehood” (verse 15).
passages.hearers:
‘Do not seal up the words.’ Daniel was told to seal his book until the time of the end. John is told the opposite. His book is for its first hearers, to be opened and understood now, ‘because the time is near’.

Verse 11 is sober. The time is near, and the book does not pretend that everyone will turn. It is a reason to take its call seriously now.

Then Jesus speaks: ‘I am coming soon, and My reward is with Me’. And he takes for himself the names God used in 1:8 and 21:6: ‘the Alpha and the Omega, the First and the Last, the Beginning and the End’. The one who is coming is the beginning and the end of all things.

‘Those who wash their robes’ have the right to the tree of life. It is the picture from 7:14: robes made white in the blood of the Lamb. The way to the tree, shut in Genesis 3, is open to those whom the Lamb has washed. Entry is a gift received, not a prize earned.

‘Outside are the dogs.’ In the ancient world ‘dogs’ was a common insult for those counted impure or shameless. Here it stands with the other wrongs for those who stay outside by their own choice. It is no label for any people or group. And the last words describe ‘everyone who loves and practices falsehood’. The book ends where it has always been: on the side of truth.
passages.ot:
‘The First and the Last’ is God's own claim in Isaiah, proof that there is no God besides him: “I am the first and I am the last, and there is no God but Me” (Isaiah 44:6). Here Jesus takes it.

And the tree of life, shut away in Genesis, is open again: in the garden God set cherubim “to guard the way to the tree of life” (Genesis 3:24).
passages.hard:
Jesus said he was coming soon. Why, so long after, has he not returned?

Christians have faced this question from the start. 2 Peter 3 answers people who were already asking it in the first century. Several answers are given, and they are held across the four ways of reading, which differ on how much of the book is already fulfilled. Preterists point out that much of Revelation concerns things that did come soon for its first hearers, such as judgment on the persecuting powers of their day, while the final return is still ahead. Many others understand ‘soon’ as describing the character of this age rather than a measured interval: since Christ's resurrection, history has entered its last stage, and his coming could be at any time, so every generation must live ready. And 2 Peter adds that God's time is not ours, and that his apparent delay is patience: “With the Lord a day is like a thousand years, and a thousand years are like a day” (2 Peter 3:8), for he is “not wanting anyone to perish but everyone to come to repentance” (2 Peter 3:9).

These notes set no date. Many dates have been set from this book, and every one has passed. Jesus said, “No one knows about that day or hour, not even the angels in heaven, nor the Son, but only the Father” (Matthew 24:36). The chapter's own emphasis is not on calculating the time but on readiness: keeping the words of the book, washing one's robes, and praying.
passages.asks: Ask whether ‘soon’ makes you anxious, or awake, or neither. Ask what it would mean for you to live as one whose robes have been washed by the Lamb. And ask where you are tempted to love falsehood, even in small things.

passages.happening:
Jesus speaks: “I, Jesus, have sent My angel to give you this testimony for the churches. I am the Root and the Offspring of David, the bright Morning Star” (verse 16).

“The Spirit and the bride say, ‘Come!’ Let the one who hears say, ‘Come!’ And let the one who is thirsty come, and the one who desires the water of life drink freely” (verse 17).
passages.hearers:
‘I, Jesus.’ The book that began as ‘the revelation of Jesus Christ’ (1:1) ends with Jesus signing it himself. And he sends it ‘for the churches’, the seven churches of Asia first, and through them every church since.

He is ‘the Root and the Offspring of David’. He is both the source of David's line and its promised heir. And he is ‘the bright Morning Star’, the planet Venus, which rises before dawn and announces the day. The night is nearly over.

Then the word ‘Come’ rings out three times. The Greek verb, erchomai, is the same verb Jesus uses for his own coming. The Spirit and the bride, the Holy Spirit and the church, say “Come!” to Jesus. The one who hears is invited to say it too. And then the word turns outward: ‘let the one who is thirsty come’. The church's prayer for Christ's coming and its invitation to the thirsty are spoken in the same breath.

‘Drink freely.’ Without price. The book that has shown judgment so plainly ends its vision with an open invitation, and it leaves that invitation open to every reader.
passages.ot:
The invitation is Isaiah's: “Come, all you who are thirsty, come to the waters; and you without money, come, buy, and eat!” (Isaiah 55:1).

The Root of David is Isaiah's promised king: “Then a shoot will spring up from the stump of Jesse, and a Branch from his roots will bear fruit” (Isaiah 11:1). And the star is Balaam's oracle: “A star will come forth from Jacob, and a scepter will arise from Israel” (Numbers 24:17).
passages.asks: Ask what you are thirsty for, and what keeps you from coming to drink freely. Ask whether your church's prayer for Christ's coming and its welcome to the thirsty belong together, as they do here. And ask whom you might say ‘Come’ to this week.

passages.happening:
John gives a warning: “I testify to everyone who hears the words of prophecy in this book: If anyone adds to them, God will add to him the plagues described in this book. And if anyone takes away from the words of this book of prophecy, God will take away his share in the tree of life and the holy city, which are described in this book” (verses 18-19).

Then the last words: “He who testifies to these things says, ‘Yes, I am coming soon.’ Amen. Come, Lord Jesus!” (verse 20).

“The grace of the Lord Jesus be with all the saints. Amen” (verse 21).
passages.hearers:
Books in John's day were copied by hand, and copyists sometimes added or dropped words. Warnings against changing a text were a known feature of ancient writings, and the Law had given one: Israel was not to add to or take away from what God commanded. John applies the same concern to his book of prophecy, which was to be read aloud in the churches. The warning is about this book's words. It was not written about the whole Bible as it was later gathered, though many Christians have applied its principle more widely.

The book ends with a promise and a prayer. Jesus says, ‘Yes, I am coming soon.’ And the church answers, “Amen. Come, Lord Jesus!” The prayer matches an Aramaic prayer of the earliest churches, maranatha, ‘Come, Lord’. Paul left it untranslated in a letter to Greek-speaking Corinth, and an early Christian manual called the Didache, probably from the late first or early second century, has the same word in its prayers after the Lord's Supper. From its first days, the church has prayed for its Lord to come.

The last word is not a warning or a vision. It is grace: ‘The grace of the Lord Jesus be with all the saints.’ The book closes like a letter, because it is one, sent to seven real churches. And so the Bible, which began with God creating the heavens and the earth, ends with grace and with a prayer for the Lord's coming.

With these words the New Testament ends, and with it the whole Bible.
passages.ot: The warning applies the Law's own: “You must not add to or subtract from what I command you, so that you may keep the commandments of the LORD your God that I am giving you” (Deuteronomy 4:2). And again: “See that you do everything I command you; do not add to it or subtract from it” (Deuteronomy 12:32).
passages.hard:
Does 22:18-19 mean that anyone who reads the Bible differently, or uses a different translation, is cursed?

No. The warning is about the words of this book of prophecy, Revelation, and about anyone who would add to them or take away from them, as copyists sometimes did by hand. It was not written about the whole Bible as it was later gathered, though many Christians have applied its principle more widely, out of reverence for Scripture.

It is not a weapon to turn on other Christians. Faithful Christians read Revelation in the four ways the book page sets out, and they hold different views of the thousand years; none of that is adding to or taking away from the book. Nor is it a word against a faithful translation of the Bible into another language, which seeks to carry the same words to new hearers. The warning guards the book against being changed. It does not license anyone to use it against a brother or sister.

And ‘I am coming soon’ is read in the ways the note on verses 10 to 15 sets out. These notes set no date.
passages.asks: Ask whether you can pray, honestly, ‘Come, Lord Jesus’, and what would have to change for that to be your deepest desire. Ask how you handle the words of Scripture: with reverence, and without turning them into a weapon. And ask what it means to you that the Bible's last word to you is grace.
